When we look at the very, very large numbers involved - had any of those things been different, by even trivial amounts, the universe would not exist. If the cosmic background radiation were off by something like 0.0001% then we'd not have a universe. Depending on how it went, we'd either have collapsed or we'd have been so diffuse that we'd have not had matter close enough for the attractive forces to work on it.

I love me some math. Mathematically, the universe is what we'd call "impossible." The odds are so astronomically low that we'd just write it off as being impossible. Yet, here we are.

I liken it to this:

Because particles are always in motion, you could put a diamond in a box and open it, close it, open it, observe it, and eventually it's statistically certain that it will have changed to a lump of coal. That's a mathematical certainty - that given enough time and enough observations, you'll encounter a time when the entire mass has changed while you weren't observing it directly. It's a certainty - assuming you had infinite years and infinite energy to keep opening, observing, and closing the box.

But, in practicality, it's impossible. Y'all can try it - just get a diamond and a box.
